# 3. Abstract

Class scheduling in the College of Engineering at Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation involves coordinating faculty assignments, class times, rooms, laboratories, and section requirements. The existing spreadsheet-based process requires repeated checking and revisions. This study documented the current workflow and scheduling concerns and established requirements for ORDIQ, a proposed standalone, AI-based scheduling decision-support system. Using an applied, developmental research design, the study examined the department's scheduling process and gathered survey responses from 23 faculty members and 349 first- and second-year engineering students. The documented scheduling cycle lasted 47 days: 15 days for initial schedule preparation, 22 days for program-level rework combined with portal encoding, and 10 days for university-level review. Among faculty respondents, 22 of 23 (95.7%) perceived a need for significant improvement; classroom conflicts were the most frequently reported problem, selected 19 times. Among student respondents, 16.6% reported requesting a schedule adjustment during the current or most recently completed semester, most commonly to change a subject schedule. These survey findings are descriptive and should not be treated as representative of the entire college. The results informed a proposed system that validates scheduling data, checks mandatory time, faculty, room, and capacity constraints, and supports staff review of candidate schedules. Because system performance has not yet been established, this study does not claim reductions in scheduling time, rework, or student adjustment requests. The findings provide a local basis for developing and evaluating a constraint-based decision-support tool while retaining human review and institutional approval.

**Keywords:** academic timetabling, class scheduling, resource allocation, decision-support system, constraint-based scheduling, engineering education

# 4. Introduction

## 4.1 Background of the Study

Academic timetable preparation requires coordinated assignment of courses, sections, instructors, students, rooms, and time periods under institutional rules. At the College of Engineering, this work relies substantially on spreadsheet-based preparation and manual review before the schedule is encoded in the university portal. For the first semester for the academic year (A.Y.) 2026-2027, the college offers seven programs: Industrial, Civil, Electrical, Mechanical, Computer, Electronics, and Geodetic Engineering. Its 44 faculty members comprise 13 part-time, 18 full-time non-permanent, 12 full-time permanent, and one visiting lecturer. A feasible schedule must satisfy course duration, faculty specialization and availability, student numbers, room and laboratory capacity and type, and section needs. A conflict in time, room, or subject assignment can therefore trigger rework. Once completed, the schedule then proceeds to institutional verification and approval, which fall outside the scope of the proposed system.

A preliminary interview with the scheduling officer describes the current process as follows: The Dean prepares a raw first-semester schedule over 15 days, including weekends. Program coordinators then rework their respective program schedules, and all 44 faculty schedules were reportedly subject to rework for the first semester of academic year 2026 to 2027. This rework takes approximately one month of eight-hour weekdays. The reworked schedules are then encoded in the portal within a day every time a rework is finished. Student schedule changes add further workload: based on the scheduling officer's estimate, that about 70% of the 903 combined first- and second-year engineering students (632 students) request a change to their schedules.

A survey of 23 out of 44 faculty identified the main causes of rework. These fall into three groups: time-related causes (faculty availability and teaching load not properly considered, overlapping class schedules, and schedule hours that do not match required contact hours), room-related causes (double-booked rooms or laboratories, and room capacity or type that does not match the class), and subject-related causes (faculty specialization not matched to subjects, changes to assignments after the schedule is drafted, and outdated curriculum information). Most of these are incompatibilities that could, in principle, be detected before the schedule is encoded.

Therefore, the problem is not only constructing a timetable but repeatedly adjusting it. Searching manually for a compatible combination of instructor, room, and time slot is slow, and conflicts are found only after they have caused rework and results to unwanted situations including delays in schedule release, sudden changes in schedules for both faculty and students, and delay beginning of classes. The volume of student change requests suggests that released schedules often do not fit students' need due to multiple reasons including unwanted subject schedule or class time and found overlapping schedules or class conflicts.

Because rooms, laboratories, and faculty load are also assigned by hand, the resulting allocation may be feasible without being efficient in comparison to a release of a feasible schedule in less than a week with minor rework on the part of few program coordinators. Timetabling of this kind is a well-studied and computationally hard combinatorial problem \[1\], \[2\], and artificial intelligence (AI)-based techniques, such as genetic algorithms, tabu search, and constraint satisfaction have long been applied to it \[3\]. However, recent reviews observe that some methods are not fully utilized in real-world settings, possibly because of limited flexibility \[2\]. This suggests a need for systems configured to the rules and workflow of a specific institution.

This study addresses that need by developing an AI-based scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering. The system validates scheduling data, generates candidate schedules, and flags incompatible assignments before portal entry, while leaving exceptions and final approval to department staff. It also seeks to improve the allocation of rooms, laboratory spaces, and faculty load, and to respect scheduling preferences approved by the college. The study's contribution is a logically configured system, evaluated against a documented current-process baseline in terms of scheduling time, conflict count, rework effort, resource utilization, and the number of student schedule change request.

## 4.2 Objectives of the Study

The main objective is to design, develop, and evaluate an AI-based automated scheduling system to support accurate and efficient class scheduling in the College of Engineering. Specifically, the study aims to:

1\. To document the existing class-scheduling workflow, participants, inputs, constraints, correction types, and time requirements in the College of Engineering.

2\. To analyze the causes of schedule rework, classified as time-, room-, and subject-related, to identify the constraints the system must detect and enforce.

3\. To design and develop a standalone system that validates scheduling data, generates feasible candidate schedules, optimizes room utilization and faculty load distribution, prioritizes stakeholder-approved preferences, and flags conflicts for human review, and presents reports and a dashboard to support review and decision-making.

4\. To evaluate the system in three stages:

4.1. Functional performance testing by the researchers;

4.2.Testing against the college's first-semester AY 2026-2027 scheduling data to assess schedule feasibility, resource utilization, and indicators of likely student change requests, and;

4.3. Pilot testing by the Dean to assess preparation effort, correction burden, and user experience, all against the prespecified criteria.

## 4.3 Significance of the Study

This study may benefit the following groups, subject to the conditions stated at the end of this section.

**Dean and program coordinators.** Automated generation and validation allow them to review candidate schedules and identify conflicts before schedules move to encoding. Rework currently takes half-a-month room, laboratory, subjects, time, and faculty scheduling plotting, combined with approximately one month of eight-hour weekdays, resulting to over 1.5-month scheduling process duration, so the study measure whether the system reduces this effort instead of assuming that it does.

**Scheduling officer.** May receive schedules that have undergone systematic pre-encoding checks for time, room, and subject conflicts. Portal entry and institutional approval remain outside the proposed system.

**Faculty.** Faculty may benefit if availability, teaching load, and subject specializations are presented accurately in the schedule, which addresses causes of rework identified in the survey.

**Students.** The study will also evaluate whether the system's schedules show fewer conflicts and unmet approved preferences, which may indicate a lower likelihood of student change requests.

**The College of Engineering.** The college may gain local evidence on the feasibility and operational value of a scheduling tool, including its effect on the use of rooms, laboratories, and faculty load and their specializations.

**The University.** The institution may adapt the proposed system once criteria and quality standards are met which can then be implemented on other college departments that may benefit the entire university in reducing scheduling efforts and minimizing conflicts in the overall process.

**Future researchers and developers.** The documented workflow, constraint classification, and evaluation criteria may serve as a reference for similar institution-specific scheduling systems.

These benefits depend on reliable input data, policy agreement, staff adoption, and satisfactory evaluation results. The study will also evaluate whether the system reduces the number of students who need to request schedule changes.

## 4.4 Scope and Limitations of the Study

The scope of the study covers class scheduling for the seven programs of the College of Engineering (Civil, Computer, Electrical, Electronics, Geodetic, Industrial, and Mechanical Engineering) within the current College of Engineering building. The proposed AI-based scheduling decision-support system uses course and section records, room and laboratory characteristics (capacity and type), time periods, faculty assignments, specializations and availability, student or section requirements, and scheduling preferences approved by the department. Using these inputs, the system validates scheduling data, generates candidate schedules, and flags conflicts for human review. The system also provides reports and a dashboard summarizing conflicts, room and laboratory utilization, and faculty load to support review and decision-making. It does not process or accommodate individual student change requests. Instead, it aims to reduce their number by producing conflict-free schedules that reflect approved preferences. The system will be tested by the researchers, then with the college's first-semester A.Y. 2026-2027 scheduling data, and finally in a pilot test by the Dean to obtain experience-based feedback. The generated schedules are not released to the students and do not replace the college's official schedule. In addition, the application supports schedule preparation before submission to the university scheduling portal. It neither replaces nor directly integrates with that portal, and it does not automate the approval of the Registrar, the Audit Office, or the Vice President for Academic Affairs and Research.

System output is limited by the completeness and accuracy of local data and by the constraints encoded and approved by the department. Outdated curriculum information and changes to faculty, subject, section, or room assignments after a schedule is drafted can be handled only to the extent that the input data are updated, and the schedule is regenerated or adjusted. Conflicting requirements may require human decision, and the system cannot guarantee that every preference will be met. Additionally, some student changes requests arise from circumstances outside the schedule, such as individual situations, and cannot be addressed by the system. The department has no official record of the student schedule change requests, the baseline is the scheduling officer's estimate. Any comparison involving change requests is therefore indicative and not a statistically established reduction. Consequently, the gathering of data is also limited in terms of the constraints involving the faculty members' presence and amount of time to collect data during the time where they are outside the university attending important events. Likewise, the project does not include scheduling for other colleges or buildings nor other universities.

Fig. 1. Conceptual Framework of the AI-based scheduling decision-support system

The study uses an input–process–output (IPO) logic with a feedback loop. Inputs comprise validated course, section, and required contact-hour data; faculty specializations, availability, and teaching load; room and laboratory characteristics; available time periods; student and section data; and the college's scheduling rules and approved preferences. The process, carried out by the AI-based scheduling decision-support system, comprises data checking and validation; constraint encoding; candidate schedule generation and optimization; conflict detection and flagging; human review and revision; and feedback and iteration. The outputs are candidate class schedules, conflict and validation reports, a dashboard and reports that support review and decision-making, and documentation of assumptions, encoded rules, and validation records.

The system's provisional predictor is the availability of an automated, constraint-based scheduling capability. The provisional outcomes are: (a) process efficiency, measured through defined staff effort and elapsed preparation time, and (b) schedule quality, assessed through hard-constraint violations, correction counts, resource utilization, indicators of likely student change requests, and satisfaction of validated soft preferences. Mandatory rules must be met for a schedule to be feasible, while preferences can be prioritized only after college stakeholders agree on their weights. Human review supplies the feedback loop for correcting inputs, changing rules, or accepting documented exceptions. Portal encoding and final approval by the Registrar, the Audit Office, and the Vice President for Academic Affairs and Research remain outside the system. The system is evaluated against the documented current-process baseline in three stages: (1) researcher testing, (2) testing with the department's first-semester A.Y. 2026–2027 scheduling data, and (3) a pilot test by the Dean.

## 4.6 Definition of Terms

**AI-based scheduling decision-support system.** The proposed standalone application that validates scheduling inputs, generates candidate timetables, and identifies constraint conflicts for authorized review. It supports, and does not replace, human decisions and institutional approval.

**Candidate schedule.** A timetable produced by the system for review by the Dean and program coordinators. It is not an approved schedule until accepted through the college's and the university's own procedures.

**Correction burden.** The amount of rework needed after a schedule is drafted, measured by the number of conflicts or corrections, the staff time spent on them, and indicators of likely students change requests.

**Dashboard**. A visual summary within the system conflicts, room and laboratory utilization, faculty load, and validation status, intended to help authorized users review candidate schedules and make decisions.

**Faculty load distribution.** The spread of teaching assignments across faculty members, assessed using measures finalized during requirements analysis.

**Hard constraint.** A mandatory scheduling rule that a feasible timetable must satisfy, such as preventing a room or faculty member from being assigned to overlapping classes.

**Optimization.** In this study, the improvement of schedule quality and resource utilization relative to the documented current-process baseline. It does not imply a mathematically global optimum.

**Pilot testing.** A trial in which the Dean uses the system with the college's first-semester AY 2026-2027 scheduling data, without releasing the generated schedules for official use, to assess the system's usability and to obtain feedback.

**Resource utilization.** The extent to which rooms, laboratories, and faculty time are used within available capacity, assessed using measures finalized during requirements analysis.

**Schedule feasibility.** The state in which all encoded hard constraints are satisfied. It does not by itself establish that preferences or schedule quality are optimal.

**Schedule quality.** The degree to which a feasible schedule meets approved soft preferences and planning objectives, assessed using measures finalized during requirements analysis.

**Scheduling-process effort.** Staff time attributable to schedule preparation and correction, recorded using a defined start and end rule and expressed in person-hours.

**Soft constraint.** A desirable but nonmandatory preference, such as avoiding a less-preferred time, whose priority must be set by the department.

# 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies

This section reviews the theories, research, patents, standards, and existing systems relevant to an AI-based scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering. It establishes the technical foundation for a constraint-based, feasibility-first design, examines how published studies and available technologies treat scheduling constraints, workload, and schedule quality, and identifies the local gap that the project intends to address.

## 5.1 Theoretical and Technical Foundations

University course timetabling is a constrained allocation problem: teaching events must be assigned to periods and rooms while respecting faculty specializations and availability, section requirements, and institutional rules. These decisions are interdependent, so a locally acceptable assignment can make another event infeasible. Timetabling surveys describe the complexity of hard and soft constraints and review exact, metaheuristic, and hybrid approaches \[2\], \[3\]. For this proposal, "AI-based" refers to constraint-based search and optimization; it does not imply machine learning.

Each required class event is assigned a time period, a room, and a qualified instructor. Hard constraints encode mandatory requirements:

- A room cannot host simultaneous classes.
- A faculty member or section cannot be assigned to overlapping events.
- Each event must receive its required duration and meeting pattern.
- A laboratory course must use a suitable laboratory room.
- Class size cannot exceed room capacity.

The college must confirm additional rules, including teaching periods, faculty-subject specializations, and weekly meeting patterns, before they are encoded. Missing or outdated rules can produce a technically feasible but unacceptable candidate. If the input constraints are infeasible, the system should report the cause rather than silently relax a mandatory rule.

Soft constraints represent preferences that may be traded off only after stakeholder approval. Candidate examples in this proposal include preferred faculty periods, avoiding evening classes for lower-year sections where feasible, minimizing excessive gaps, balancing room use, and distributing faculty load. Constraint-handling approaches distinguish mandatory rules from preferences \[4\]. The final set and priority of soft constraints remain subject to requirements analysis; no preference should override a hard constraint without an authorized, documented exception.

Mixed-integer programming can represent assignment and resource constraints explicitly. Rappos et al. used a feasible-solution stage followed by local improvement in a competition problem that also included student-to-class allocation \[5\]. That benchmark design is informative about staged optimization, but individual student allocation is outside this proposal's scope. A suitable design sequence is to seek hard-constraint feasibility first, then improve candidates against stakeholder-approved preferences.

The system should make candidate assignments, detected conflicts, unmet preferences, and the reasons for each warning reviewable. Multi-criteria timetabling research illustrates that criteria and decision levels can differ; some models also include individual student assignments, which this project excludes \[6\]. Whether the prototype uses a lexicographic hierarchy or agreed weights must be decided during requirements analysis and documented for staff review. The technical foundation is therefore a transparent constraint model, feasibility checks, preference-based improvement after stakeholder approval, and human review.

## 5.2 Review of Related Literature

**Automated scheduling.** Automated timetabling research includes exact models, constraint-based methods, metaheuristics, and hybrids. The university course-timetabling survey by Chen et al. describes the prevalence of metaheuristic and hybrid approaches and notes that limited flexibility may constrain uptake in real-world settings \[2\], \[3\]. This literature supports explicit local rule encoding and testing; it does not establish which solver will fit this college or prove that automation alone improves schedule quality.

**Constraint-handling.** Constraint-handling rules provide one way to represent mandatory conditions and preferences within a scheduling approach \[4\]. Mixed-integer programming provides another explicit formulation: Rappos et al. report a feasible-first method followed by local improvement and benchmark performance in the International Timetabling Competition 2019 \[5\]. The competition result is computational evidence for those instances, not evidence of local usability, staff-time savings, or fit with the department's rules.

**Customization.** Customization matters because institutions differ in their constraints and workflows. Algethami and Laesanklang model faculty-course assignments, specializations, preferences, and workload in a pre-registration setting \[7\]. Dunke and Nickel examine customized multi-level, multi-criteria planning, including individual assignments \[6\]. These studies help identify possible dimensions for requirements analysis, but the proposed prototype remains at the section, faculty, and room level and does not allocate individual students.

**Algorithm performance.** Algorithm studies report results on defined instances rather than end-to-end administrative outcomes. Song et al. found feasible solutions for 58 of 60 benchmark instances with an iterated local-search method \[8\]; Thepphakorn and Pongcharoen compared Cuckoo Search strategies on 11 engineering-faculty instances \[9\]. Such results demonstrate computational approaches in their tested settings only. They do not establish that either method is suitable for the department's data or that a particular runtime translates into reduced coordinator effort.

**Operational efficiency.** Evidence about operational efficiency should be separated from solver performance. Abdennadher and Marte describe a Munich prototype and report minutes of processing compared with manual days in that setting \[4\]. Stallaert reports an operational university case in which administrators used automated scheduling for three years and described comparable schedules as being prepared faster than manually \[10\]. Both are context-specific reports; neither provides a local estimate for this department. The present evaluation should therefore record elapsed time and person-hours by process stage, alongside solver runtime and correction effort.

**Real-world scheduling cases.** Real-world problem descriptions also differ in their decision scope and data. Rudová, Müller, and Müllerová analyze 30 competition cases combining student sectioning with time and room assignment \[11\]. Their work illustrates variation across institutions, but those benchmark cases are not a direct comparator for a single college's pre-portal workflow. The proposed evaluation should use locally verified rules and a documented current-process baseline.

**Schedule-quality measures.** Studies of schedule quality provide candidate measures rather than a ready-made local objective. Tavakoli et al. report a course-timetabling case study using lecturer and course-related measures \[12\]. Palma and Bornhardt consider section balance and schedule flexibility in a curriculum-based model, including a real-case comparison with a manual schedule \[13\]. These examples make section balance and preference satisfaction reasonable topics for stakeholder review, but their case-specific results should not be generalized to this project.

**Faculty and room constraints.** Faculty assignments, room suitability, capacity, and time conflicts are directly relevant to the department's stated scheduling problem. Research on faculty-course assignment constraints supports representing specializations, availability, and load explicitly \[7\]. The literature does not determine the college's preferred load distribution or establish that any one measure should dominate. The system should report feasibility separately from preference satisfaction, and staff should review any trade-offs.

**Schedule-quality criteria.** Schedule quality is multidimensional. A candidate must first satisfy approved hard constraints; among feasible candidates, stakeholders may consider room and laboratory suitability, faculty availability and workload, section conflicts, and approved preferences. The preliminary faculty survey and scheduling-officer interview identify local issues for investigation, but neither establishes population-level priorities or a validated weighting scheme.

**Fairness.** Fairness may also matter if the department identifies a defensible objective, such as the distribution of undesirable time periods. Mühlenthaler and Wanka study the distribution of undesirable soft-constraint violations in academic timetabling \[14\]. Their work motivates asking stakeholders whether such a criterion is relevant; it does not mean that this proposal has selected a fairness measure or defined the groups to compare.

**Student-level allocation.** This study does not optimize individual student schedules. Research that combines student sectioning with room and time assignment \[11\] or considers individual courses of study \[6\] addresses a broader or later allocation stage. Here, section-level enrollment and year information may inform candidate schedules, but the prototype will not assign named or individual students to sections. Any future expansion would require separate requirements, data, privacy review, and evaluation.

**Evaluation measures.** Accordingly, evaluation should distinguish hard-constraint violations from unmet soft preferences, documented exceptions, resource-use measures, and staff correction effort. Benchmark feasibility, solver speed, or an aggregate score alone would not establish operational benefit. The definitions of errors, approved preferences, and any group-level comparisons must be settled with college stakeholders before testing.

**Local validation.** The literature provides design options and candidate evaluation dimensions, not a predetermined solver, objective weight, or expected benefit. The local study must verify its input data, confirm the department's rules, document the current workflow, and test whether staff can interpret and use the generated reports. No reduction in preparation time, rework, or student change requests is claimed before evaluation.

## 5.3 Review of Patent Literature

Patent literature was reviewed as a preliminary scan of examples of class-scheduling technology, not as a systematic patent search. The records in Table I were checked against public patent-database pages. They do not establish novelty, patentability, or freedom to operate; those questions require a broader search and appropriate legal review.

For the prototype, design requirements should be derived from verified department needs: display the reason for each detected conflict, distinguish mandatory rules from preferences, show the effect of revisions, and retain a record of approved rule priorities.

## 5.4 Applicable Engineering Standards and Regulations

ISO/IEC 25010:2023 and ISO/IEC 25012:2008 may guide the selection of software- and data-quality criteria relevant to the proposed scheduling decision-support system \[17\], \[18\]. The evaluation will use criteria that are relevant to the prototype and defined as observable measures in the methods section—for example, correct handling of approved scheduling constraints, validation of input data, and system response time.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 may guide how stakeholder needs and system requirements are elicited, documented, and checked for consistency \[19\]. The research team will tailor this guidance to the project's scope, including the college's approved scheduling rules and reporting needs.

The project will consider applicable university quality procedures under the university's ISO 9001-based quality-management system \[20\]. This may include documenting approved requirements and scheduling rules, recording validation and test results, and tracking revisions, exceptions, and corrective actions. This is project-level alignment with applicable university procedures; it is not a claim that the prototype is independently certified or conforms to all ISO 9001 requirements. The applicable edition should be confirmed with the university's quality-management office before finalizing reference \[20\].

The proposed system schedules sections, faculty, and rooms; it does not assign individual students to sections. Where feasible, student enrollment should therefore be represented by section-level counts or requirements rather than individual student records. If identifiable faculty or student personal information is collected or used, the research team must follow applicable institutional ethics and data-protection requirements, including Republic Act No. 10173, the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012 \[21\]. The protocol should specify the purpose and scope of data use, data minimization, access controls, secure storage, retention, and safeguards for coded or aggregated information, subject to university review and authorization.

## 5.5 Existing Technologies and Systems

Relevant technologies include constraint-based scheduling, mathematical-programming models, heuristic search, and interactive timetable tools. Published work addresses constraint handling \[4\], mixed-integer scheduling \[5\], faculty-course assignment \[7\], and section balance \[13\]; the patent records provide additional examples of class scheduling and adjustment \[15\], \[16\]. These sources address different decision scopes and do not demonstrate that a particular package is suitable for the department. The current local workflow uses spreadsheets and the university portal, whose capabilities must be confirmed directly with the department. The proposed system is standalone and supports preparation before portal entry; it does not integrate with the portal, assign individual students, or approve schedules.

For requirements analysis, candidate systems can be compared on support for time, room, and faculty constraints; laboratory type and capacity; separation of hard and soft rules; conflict explanations; staff-controlled revision; import or export; auditability; response time; and setup effort. These are comparison criteria, not confirmed features of a selected product. No software package or solver is selected until data, implementation requirements, licensing, and available technical resources have been reviewed.

## 5.6 Synthesis of the Review

The reviewed literature supports investigating a transparent, feasibility-first scheduling process that separates mandatory constraints from stakeholder-approved preferences and leaves final review to college staff. Published algorithm results concern their tested instances; operational reports are limited to the institutions studied \[4\], \[8\]–\[10\]. Other work helps identify faculty-assignment, section-balance, and possible fairness dimensions \[7\], \[13\], \[14\], while competition cases show that timetabling problems vary across institutions \[11\]. Preliminary patent records are examples only \[15\], \[16\]. The proposal's listed standards require edition and applicability checks before detailed use \[17\]–\[20\], and data handling requires institutional review under applicable law \[21\]. The local gap is to translate verified college rules into a standalone pre-portal decision-support prototype and evaluate feasibility, preference satisfaction, resource use, preparation effort, corrections, and user experience against a documented baseline.

# 6. Methods and Procedures

## 6.1 Research Design

The study is applied research because it responds to a documented local scheduling problem, and developmental research because it will design, build, and evaluate a software system. The work will proceed from descriptive process analysis to requirements specification, iterative prototype development, and system evaluation. At proposal stage, only the scheduling-officer interview figures have been supplied; faculty and student baseline data and the proposed system's performance results are not yet available.

Evaluation should compare the current process with system-assisted scheduling on the same or closely matched schedule inputs where feasible. If a single semester's data and schedule cycle are available, use paired comparisons at the schedule or program level; otherwise report descriptive prototype tests and usability findings without implying a causal effect.

## 6.2 Research Environment

The study is situated in the College of Engineering at Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation (MSEUF), Lucena City. The system scope is the seven programs and the current College of Engineering building. Department personnel prepare schedules through the existing spreadsheet-based workflow and submit schedules to the university's official portal for encoding and subsequent institutional review. Program coordinators, the Dean, scheduling personnel, faculty, and students are relevant stakeholders. The application is planned as a standalone tool used before portal encoding.

## 6.3 Procedures

The procedure for this study followed a systematic, step-by-step process, beginning with the collection of relevant information and the identification and analysis of existing class scheduling problems. Based on the findings, appropriate solutions were formulated, and a development plan for the decision-support system was established. The process then proceeded to the system's design and development, followed by implementation and validation to assess its functionality and effectiveness in addressing the identified scheduling problems.

### 6.3.1 **Data-Gathering Plan**

The data-gathering process was designed to identify the existing problems in the class scheduling process of the College of Engineering and establish the requirements for the proposed decision-support system. Interviews with the Dean and the scheduling officer were conducted to obtain information about the current scheduling practices, encountered difficulties, and considerations involved in faculty and classroom assignments. These interviews provided the initial context for the study and helped identify the issues requiring further investigation.

Survey questionnaires were also administered to faculty members and students. Printed questionnaires were distributed to faculty members, while an online questionnaire was used to gather responses from students. The instruments consisted of multiple-choice questions, open-ended questions and rating-scale questions. The questions covered the respondents' profiles, experiences with the existing scheduling process, satisfaction levels, encountered problems, feedback, and suggested improvements. The collected responses were used to identify recurring scheduling issues and determine the functional requirements of the proposed system.

For the faculty survey, the target sample consisted of 30 out of the 44 faculty members in the College of Engineering. Due to the limited availability of some faculty members, the research team sought to obtain responses from as many faculty members as possible. If the target sample could not be achieved, the actual number of respondents would be reported, together with the corresponding response rate and sampling limitations. This approach allowed the researchers to document the available faculty feedback without assuming that a smaller sample automatically satisfied the intended margin of error.

For the student survey, the population consisted of 903 first- and second-year engineering students. Using Slovin's formula with a 5% margin of error, the required sample size was calculated as follows:

$$
n=\frac{N}{1+Ne^2}
$$

(1)

$$
n=\frac{903}{1+(903)({0.05)}^2}
$$

$$
n=277.14 (approx. 278)
$$

Therefore, the target sample was set at 278 students. The survey aimed to determine the reasons for student requests for schedule changes and identify the problems they encountered with the existing scheduling process. The selection of respondents was to be conducted using a Cluster sampling method to ensure that the student population was adequately represented.

The data-gathering activities were allocated a period of eight weeks: three weeks for approvals, 2 weeks for interview on the stakeholders including analysis on department's workflow, and three weeks for respondent survey. In parallel, the research team sought authorization through the appropriate university office to access the department portal and obtain relevant scheduling records. Subject to the approved scope of access, these records would be used as input data for developing, testing, and validating the proposed decision-support system. The records would support the assessment of the system's ability to assist in scheduling decisions and resource allocation. The findings from the interviews, surveys, and authorized portal records would then be consolidated to establish the system requirements and evaluate the proposed solution.

### 6.3.2 **Analysis Plan**

The analysis plan focuses on reviewing the technical requirements, applicable standards, and operational constraints relevant to the development of the proposed class scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering. The review will establish the necessary system functions, data requirements, operating conditions, and limitations that must be considered in designing the proposed solution.

The technical requirements will be examined by identifying the scheduling data needed by the system, including faculty profiles and specializations, teaching assignments, course offerings, and classroom and laboratory availability. The required system functions, data-processing procedures, and expected outputs will also be identified to establish how the system will support scheduling decisions and identify potential conflicts. Relevant software, hardware, and data-access requirements will be considered in determining the system's technical specifications and overall design.

Applicable university policies, departmental scheduling procedures, and relevant technical and data privacy requirements will also be reviewed to ensure that the proposed system follows established scheduling rules and information-handling requirements. Particular attention will be given to faculty specialization requirements, teaching assignments, room capacity, and resource availability, as these factors may affect the feasibility of schedule allocation.

Finally, the operational and technical constraints affecting system development and implementation will be assessed. These may include restrictions on accessing the existing department portal, the availability and completeness of scheduling records, limitations in faculty and classroom resources, and the time and technical resources available for development. The findings from these reviews will serve as the basis for defining the system requirements, establishing the design specifications, and determining the appropriate scope and functionality of the proposed decision-support system.

The findings from these activities will be consolidated to determine the system requirements, design specifications, and implementation limitations. These outputs will provide the basis for the subsequent design and development of the proposed system.

### 6.3.3 **Design and Development Plan**

The design and development plan describes the process of translating the identified technical requirements, scheduling rules, and operational constraints into a functional class scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering. The development process will focus on establishing the system specifications, designing the system components, and integrating the necessary functions to support scheduling decisions and resource allocation.

The design specifications will be established based on the results of the analysis, including the required scheduling data, faculty specialization requirements, teaching assignments, classroom and laboratory availability, and applicable scheduling rules. These specifications will define the system's required inputs, processing procedures, decision rules, and outputs. A system architecture diagram, process flowchart, and input-process-output model may be prepared to illustrate the relationships among the system components and the flow of scheduling information.

The development stage will involve preparing the necessary system models and logical procedures for processing scheduling data, identifying conflicts, and generating scheduling recommendations. Appropriate programming tools, software components, and data-management methods will be selected based on the established specifications and available technical resources. The identified functions will then be programmed and integrated into the proposed system to ensure that the input data, scheduling rules, processing procedures, and outputs operate as intended.

The completed system design and its integrated components will serve as the basis for subsequent testing and validation. The developed system will be evaluated to determine whether it satisfies the established functional requirements and supports the scheduling needs of the College of Engineering.

### 6.3.4 **Evaluation/ Validation Plan**

The evaluation and validation plan focuses on determining whether the developed class scheduling decision-support system meets the established technical requirements and addresses the scheduling problems identified in the College of Engineering. The system will be evaluated through functional testing, verification of scheduling constraints, and assessment of its usability and practical applicability to the existing scheduling process.

Functional testing will be conducted to determine whether the system processes the required scheduling data correctly, identifies potential conflicts, and generates scheduling recommendations based on the defined rules and constraints. The resulting schedules will be examined to verify compliance with applicable requirements, including faculty specialization, teaching assignments, classroom and laboratory availability, and other relevant scheduling policies. Where appropriate, the system's outputs will be compared with existing scheduling records or manually verified scheduling scenarios to assess the accuracy and consistency of its results.

The system's practical usefulness will also be evaluated using appropriate feedback from the intended users, such as the scheduling officer and other authorized personnel involved in class scheduling. Their feedback will be used to assess the system's usability, clarity of outputs, and suitability for supporting scheduling decisions. If baseline data on scheduling preparation time and revisions are available, these may also be compared with results obtained using the developed system to examine potential improvements in process efficiency.

Finally, the evaluation results, identified limitations, testing records, and recommended improvements will be documented. Relevant system diagrams, specifications, test cases, results, and user feedback will be compiled to provide evidence of the system's performance and the extent to which it meets the objectives of the study.

## 6.4 Design Concept

![A calendar with a brain inside

Description automatically generated](data:image/jpeg;base64,) The proposed design is an AI-assisted, spreadsheet-based class scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering, named ORDIQ, with the tagline "Order Meets Intelligence." The system is designed to support the preparation, checking, generation, and review of class schedules while retaining authorized personnel's responsibility for reviewing and approving the final timetable.

Fig. 3. ORDIQ Application Logo

Figure 3 illustrates the ORDIQ logo combines a calendar and a stylized artificial intelligence brain to represent the integration of class scheduling and intelligent decision support. The maroon and orange color scheme establishes the application's visual identity, while the calendar symbolizes timetable organization, and the brain represents AI-assisted analysis and decision-making. These elements reflect the system's tagline, "Order Meets Intelligence."

1. **Overview of the Proposed System**

The proposed system will be developed as a standalone scheduling application featuring a spreadsheet-based workspace, an integrated AI Assistant, a dashboard, and reporting functions. Its interface will provide centralized access to academic data and scheduling tools, allowing authorized users to manage scheduling information, identify conflicts, generate candidate timetables, and review resource allocation. The application will support both the validation of existing schedules and the generation of alternative schedules based on approved constraints. Final approval and encoding into the existing academic portal will remain outside the system's direct scope.

2. **Spreadsheet-Based Workspace**

The main workspace will organize faculty, courses and sections, rooms and laboratories, time periods, and schedules into editable tables. The faculty data view will include information such as faculty identification, specialization, teaching load, availability, preferences, and status. Data-entry controls, search, filtering, and import and export options will support the management and review of scheduling records. Validation rules will identify missing, invalid, or inconsistent information before schedule generation.

![A screenshot of a computer

Description automatically generated](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 4. Proposed ORDIQ Application Interface

Figure 4 shows the proposed interface presents the system's main dashboard, spreadsheet-based data workspace, weekly schedule preview, system analytics, and integrated AI Assistant. The navigation sidebar provides access to faculty, courses and sections, rooms and laboratories, schedules, rules and preferences, and reports. Dashboard indicators summarize scheduling information, while the AI Assistant supports users in identifying conflicts and requesting schedule improvements.

The interface is designed to consolidate scheduling activities within a single workspace. The spreadsheet-based layout supports the management and review of academic data, while the dashboard and analytics provide an overview of scheduling conditions. The AI Assistant complements these functions by helping users interpret issues and access scheduling operations. Together, these components are intended to support a more organized scheduling process while retaining human review and approval of final schedules.

3. **Integrated AI Assistant**

A persistent AI Assistant panel will be positioned beside the main workspace, allowing users to issue supported natural-language commands without leaving the current view. Users may request conflict checks, workload summaries, explanations of scheduling issues, room-utilization reviews, and candidate schedule generation. The AI Assistant will interpret requests and explain results, while the constraint-based scheduling engine will perform the actual validation and timetable-generation operations. Changes to important records and schedules will require user review and confirmation.

4. **Dashboard and Reporting Functions**

The dashboard will provide an overview of scheduling status through indicators such as the number of classes scheduled, detected conflicts, faculty workload balance, and room utilization. The finalized interface will also include a weekly timetable preview, system analytics, and a summary of conflicts requiring attention. Reporting functions will present validation findings, candidate schedules, unresolved constraints, and scheduling summaries. Displayed indicators will be based on available data and defined calculation methods; illustrative values in the design mockup will not be treated as verified results.

5. **Proposed System Architecture**

The system will consist of connected components for data management, validation, scheduling, user interaction, reporting, and export. The spreadsheet workspace will manage academic records, the validation module will check data quality, and the constraint-based scheduling engine will evaluate existing schedules and generate candidate timetables. The AI Assistant will interpret user requests and explain results, while the dashboard and reporting module will present relevant indicators and findings. An export module will prepare reviewed schedules for encoding into the existing academic portal. The application will operate independently without assuming direct portal integration.

6. **Scheduling Constraints and Priorities**

The scheduling engine will distinguish between hard constraints and soft preferences. Hard constraints, such as faculty availability, faculty and room conflicts, room capacity and suitability, required course contact hours, and approved calendar restrictions, must be satisfied for a schedule to be considered feasible. Soft preferences, such as preferred teaching periods and workload distribution, may be used to compare feasible alternatives based on priorities approved by the department. If no feasible schedule can be generated, the system will report the limitation rather than silently relax mandatory requirements.

7. **Proposed User Workflow**

The proposed workflow will begin with entering or importing academic data, followed by data validation and the checking of existing schedules or generation of candidate timetables. The system will display conflicts, unmet preferences, and other relevant findings through the spreadsheet workspace, dashboard, AI Assistant, and reports. Authorized users may correct data, revise scheduling criteria, and compare alternatives before reviewing and approving a selected schedule. The approved timetable may then be exported for encoding into the existing portal.

8. **Data Management, Export, and User Control**

The system will use structured records to support consistent validation of faculty, courses, sections, rooms, and schedules. Import and export functions will be designed according to the data formats required by the department. Access to scheduling information will be limited to authorized users, and the application will distinguish original records from proposed changes and generated schedules. Important changes will require confirmation to support data integrity and human oversight.

9. **System Evaluation and Validation**

The proposed system will be evaluated through functional testing, testing using available first-semester Academic Year 2026–2027 scheduling data, and pilot testing with the Dean or other authorized personnel. Evaluation may consider schedule feasibility, conflict detection, faculty workload compliance, room utilization, schedule preparation and revision effort, and user-perceived usability. Performance claims will be based on defined evaluation criteria and actual test results rather than the visual interface alone.

10. **Design Decisions Requiring Confirmation**

The final implementation will require confirmation of the department's mandatory scheduling constraints, preference priorities, spreadsheet fields, AI Assistant permissions, import and export formats, user access requirements, and evaluation criteria. These details will be established with the appropriate department personnel and project supervisor before implementation.

# 7. Results and Discussion

This section presents and discusses the findings from the interviews, documented scheduling workflow, time-study records, and surveys administered to faculty members and first- and second-year engineering students. The results are examined in relation to the study objectives of documenting the existing scheduling process, identifying recurring scheduling problems and their potential causes, and deriving requirements for an AI-based scheduling decision-support system. The findings describe the current process and provide a basis for system design and subsequent evaluation; they do not establish that the proposed system has already improved scheduling performance.

1. **Existing Process and Challenges of Department Scheduling**

The existing scheduling process was examined through interviews with the Dean and scheduling officer and review of the recorded workflow. The analysis focused on the sequence of schedule preparation, portal encoding, conflict checking, program-level revisions, and university-level review. These findings were used to identify the operational constraints that should be addressed by the proposed decision-support system**.**

Fig. 5. Current Scheduling Process of the Department

Figure 5 illustrates the existing scheduling process of the College of Engineering, as documented through interviews with the department dean and scheduling officer. The process begins with the dean manually preparing the department schedule using Microsoft Excel, considering faculty specialization and availability, course subjects, time blocks, classrooms, and laboratories. The schedule is then forwarded to the scheduling officer, who encodes the information into the university portal and manually checks for scheduling conflicts. When conflicts are detected, the scheduling officer notifies the concerned program coordinators, who manually revise their respective program schedules. The revised information is then returned for further processing and checking. Once no conflicts are detected, the schedule report is submitted through the portal for review by the Registrar, followed by endorsement to the Audit Department and the Office of the Vice President for Academic and Research Affairs (OVPAR). The university processors then verify the submitted schedule and determine whether it is accepted. If the schedule is rejected, the department must make the necessary revisions and resubmit the report, potentially extending the overall processing time. These review and verification stages follow established procedures and processing periods that are beyond the department's direct control.

The interviews further revealed three major challenges that contribute to the complexity and delays of the existing scheduling process, ranked by the department dean and scheduling officer as follows: (1) faculty specialization, (2) time gaps between subjects, and (3) classroom and laboratory utilization based on capacity.

**Faculty specialization.** Faculty specialization was identified as the most challenging scheduling consideration because each faculty member must be assigned subjects aligned with their qualifications and area of specialization. Differences in faculty teaching loads, specializations, and assigned subject types further complicate the allocation process, requiring considerable effort to develop a feasible schedule.

**Time gaps between subjects.** Unexpected gaps between subjects may become apparent after schedules have been prepared or published, requiring further adjustments. The scheduling officer also reported that students may begin enrolling while the schedules are still being encoded into the academic portal. This situation creates additional constraints because enrollment may begin before the schedules have been finalized, potentially complicating subsequent revisions.

**Classroom and laboratory utilization based on capacity.** Another challenge involves assigning student sections to appropriate classrooms and laboratories according to enrollment and room capacity. Based on the information gathered, lecture rooms accommodate at least 40 students, while laboratory rooms accommodate at least 30 students. Although the department considers its available facilities sufficient, the limited number of rooms requires careful coordination of room assignments, student sections, and time slots to avoid conflicts and capacity-related issues.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the primary improvement opportunity lies in optimizing the scheduling and allocation of existing academic resources rather than simply increasing the number of available rooms. Improving the coordination of faculty assignments, subject time slots, student sections, and room utilization may reduce scheduling conflicts and unnecessary revisions. A decision-support system that identifies potential conflicts before submission could help the department prepare more accurate schedules and minimize avoidable rework. However, the university's required review and verification stages would remain necessary, and their established processing periods would still need to be considered in the overall scheduling timeline.

Table III summarizes the recorded durations for the existing scheduling process. The total recorded duration is 47 days, consisting of 15 days for preparation of the initial scheduling matrix, 22 days for program-schedule rework combined with portal encoding and re-encoding, and 10 days for the subsequent university-level review stages. The 10-day review period comprises three days for the Registrar, four days for the Audit Department, and three days for the Office of the Vice President for Academic and Research Affairs (OVPAR). These figures should be retained only if they match the source records and the process stages were measured using consistent start and end points.

The first 37 days represent 78.7% of the recorded 47-day duration, while the university-level review stages account for the remaining 10 days, or 21.3%. These percentages describe the distribution of recorded elapsed time; they do not represent the percentage of waste or the amount of time that could necessarily be saved. In particular, the 22-day entry combines rework and portal encoding, so the time attributable to each activity cannot be separated from the available data. The results therefore indicate an opportunity to improve early validation and reduce avoidable revisions, but they do not quantify potential time savings.

Research on university course timetabling describes scheduling as a constrained allocation problem in which multiple requirements must be considered together \[22\]. In the College of Engineering, these requirements include faculty specialization and availability, teaching assignments, room and laboratory capacity, section schedules, and required contact hours. A decision-support system could help staff identify conflicts before portal submission. However, the extent to which it reduces preparation time or revisions must be established through testing against the documented manual baseline. The recorded 47 days should also be identified as calendar days or working days, and the study should clarify whether any process stages overlap.

2. **Results of Survey**

The survey was conducted within the College of Engineering. Printed questionnaires were distributed to faculty members, while online questionnaires were administered to first- and second-year engineering students. A total of 23 faculty members responded from a population of 44, equivalent to 52.27% of the faculty population. The student survey received 349 responses, exceeding the stated target of 278. The results are presented descriptively to identify reported scheduling experiences and requirements. Because participation depended on respondent availability and the student survey covered only first- and second-year students, the findings should not automatically be generalized to every faculty member or student in the department.

Fig. 13. Process Improvement Voting

![A diagram of a pie chart

Description automatically generated](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 14. Process Improvement Voting

Figure 12 summarizes faculty members' ratings of their experiences with the existing scheduling system. The responses include agreement, neutrality, and disagreement across the presented statements. The results therefore indicate varied experiences rather than unanimous dissatisfaction. The interpretation should remain tied to the wording and response scale of each survey item, and the figure should display legible labels and counts or percentages.

As shown in the process-improvement results, 22 of the 23 faculty respondents answered that the existing scheduling system needs significant improvement, while one respondent answered no. Thus, 95.7% of the participating faculty members indicated a perceived need for improvement. The improvement aspects shown in the associated figures include faculty availability and assignment, room or laboratory assignment, schedule preparation, and schedule coordination. These findings support further development of a decision-support tool, but they do not by themselves demonstrate that an AI-based system will be effective.

![A graph with blue bars

Description automatically generated](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 15. Problems Encountered in the Scheduling System

Figure 15 shows the problems reported by faculty members in the existing scheduling process. Classroom conflicts were selected 19 times, schedule errors 11 times, time lapses 11 times, specialization mismatch seven times, and other problems once. Classroom conflicts were therefore the most frequently selected issue, while schedule errors and time lapses were tied for the next-highest count. Because the item allowed multiple selections, these values are selection counts and should not be interpreted as mutually exclusive categories or summed to estimate a proportion of respondents. The results suggest that the system should check room and laboratory double-booking, time-slot overlap, and schedule consistency while continuing to enforce faculty-specialization requirements as a mandatory assignment rule.

![A graph with blue bars

Fig. 17. Frequency of Faculty Reworking on their Schedule

![A graph of blue rectangular bars

Fig. 18. Time-related Causes

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 19. Room-related Causes

![A graph of blue squares

Description automatically generated](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 20. Room-related Causes

For the frequency of errors or conflicts in faculty schedules, six respondents selected "Rarely," 11 selected "Sometimes," and six selected "Often"; no respondent selected "Never" or "Very Often." For the frequency of schedule revisions or rework, five respondents selected "Rarely," 11 selected "Sometimes," and seven selected "Often"; again, no respondent selected "Never" or "Very Often." These results show that all 23 participating faculty members reported encountering errors or conflicts and schedule rework at least rarely. The modal response for both items was "Sometimes." The findings indicate recurring issues within the respondent group, but they do not quantify the time or cost associated with each revision.

The reported causes span time, room, and subject-related constraints. Time-related selections included overlapping schedules involving faculty, year levels, or sections (15), faculty availability or teaching load not being properly considered (12), and schedule hours not matching required contact hours (six). Room-related selections included room or laboratory availability and double-booking (14), and a mismatch between room capacity or type and the class or subject (12). Subject-related selections included changes in faculty, subject, section, or room after the draft schedule was prepared (15), outdated or incorrect subject information (seven), and faculty-specialization mismatch (six). Since these were multiple-response items, the counts are not mutually exclusive. Collectively, they support the need for reliable input data, early conflict checking, and revalidation whenever an affected assignment changes.

![Forms response chart. Question title: 6. During the current or most recently completed semester, have you requested a change or adjustment to your class schedule at the College of Engineering Dean&apos;s Office?. Number of responses: 349 responses.](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 21. Number of Student Schedule-Change Requests

![Forms response chart. Question title: 8. What type(s) of schedule adjustment did you request? Select all that apply.. Number of responses: 58 responses.](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 22. Types of Schedule-Change Requests

The student questionnaire received 349 responses from first- and second-year engineering students. In the schedule-change question, 16.6% of respondents answered yes and 83.4% answered no. Based on 349 responses, these percentages correspond approximately to 58 yes responses and 291 no responses; the exact counts should be confirmed using the raw survey export before submission. The types-of-adjustment chart is based on the 58 responses and allows multiple selections. The most frequently selected adjustment was a change in subject schedule (39 selections, 67.2%), followed by resolution of overlapping schedules (17, 29.3%), family or personal circumstances (14, 24.1%), change of instructor or class section (13, 22.4%), adding or dropping subjects (10, 17.2%), and change of room or laboratory (four, 6.9%).

The survey result differs substantially from the scheduling officer's approximate estimate that 70% of 903 first- and second-year students request schedule changes. These values come from different sources and should not be combined or treated as equivalent measures. The available information does not establish whether the discrepancy results from different definitions of a schedule-change request, different reporting periods, different populations, or recall and response differences. Unless the researchers can verify a common definition and reporting period, the paper should report both figures with their sources and explicitly state that they are not directly comparable.

The student responses indicate that subject-time compatibility and overlapping schedules are relevant concerns. However, requests related to family or personal circumstances and adding or dropping subjects may not be preventable through timetable optimization. The student results should therefore inform the system's conflict-checking requirements without implying that every schedule-change request can or should be eliminated.

3. **Analysis**

**![A diagram of a schedule

Description automatically generated](data:image/png;base64,)**

Fig. 23. Ishikawa Diagram of Scheduling Rework

.

The effect examined in the Ishikawa analysis is repeated schedule corrections and prolonged preparation of a feasible department timetable. The interview, time-study, and survey findings indicate potential contributing causes in several connected areas: people and assignment information, scheduling methods, time and section constraints, room and laboratory resources, source-data accuracy, and post-draft changes. The diagram organizes these reported factors for analysis; it does not prove that each factor independently causes rework. A fishbone diagram is commonly used to organize potential causes of a defined problem and support further investigation \[23\].

![](data:image/png;base64,)Fig. 24. Why-Why Analysis Identified Scheduling Problem

The proposed decision-support system should therefore validate required input fields, check mandatory constraints, flag overlapping assignments, identify the records involved in each conflict, and recheck affected assignments after changes. Final scheduling decisions and exceptions should remain subject to authorized department personnel.

**Synthesis and implications for system requirements**

The results identify recurring problems involving room conflicts, schedule errors, time lapses, workload and availability, required contact hours, and changes to scheduling information after the initial draft. The interviews emphasize faculty specialization as a difficult planning constraint, while faculty respondents most frequently reported classroom conflicts. These findings are not necessarily contradictory: the interviews describe perceived difficulty in constructing the overall timetable, whereas the survey records problems experienced by individual faculty members. The system should prioritize mandatory constraint checking, data validation, and revalidation after changes. The study should evaluate the prototype using documented criteria such as the number of detected conflicts, the number of unresolved hard-constraint violations, the number of revisions required, preparation and review time, and user feedback. No performance improvement should be claimed until these measures have been tested against the existing process.

In summary, the findings have several limitations. The faculty survey included 23 of 44 faculty members, and the student survey covered first- and second-year students only. The reported 16.6% student schedule-change result differs from the scheduling officer's approximate 70% estimate, and the available information does not establish that the figures use the same definition, population, or reporting period. The time-study record also combines schedule rework and portal encoding into a single 22-day entry, preventing the duration of each activity from being separated. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results and when designing the subsequent system evaluation.

Further, the results describe a manual, multi-stage scheduling process with a recorded duration of 47 days and recurring problems associated with time, room, and subject constraints. The findings support developing a decision-support system that assists authorized personnel in validating scheduling data and identifying conflicts before submission. The system's actual effect on preparation time, rework, and schedule quality must be determined through functional testing and comparison with the documented manual baseline.
